results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The reverse outline (58 body units plus 3 intro callouts) lists the spec's controlling ideas in the spec's order; every unit maps to its aligned spec paragraph. Units marked two_ideas (Things ¶2, Eva ¶12, In Practice ¶2, the Take Away lists) carry pairs the spec itself joins in one controlling idea or subordinate support (e.g. IFRS 15 revenue timing explains why finance cares about delivery). Take Away ¶2 adds a third context-dependent bullet (stock freshness) beyond p56, without changing the unit's controlling idea.
Each aligned unit develops one controlling idea; dense units (p45 payment confirmation, p17 requirements, p35 accounting) stay on a single idea with supporting detail.
Every unit serves a supporting claim S1-S6 or the intro/conclusion roles declared in the spec; no orphan paragraphs.

results.draft_locus: Why the Joins Are Where Things Break ¶6 (requirements table)
results.quote: A refund issued by hand in the PSP console: the Double Refund.
results.finding: The requirements table files the Double Refund under 'If the receiver is down', but the Duplicated paragraph explains it as two senders with no shared record; the table never says what outage was involved, so the evidence points two ways (cold_AC-3 reader could not reconcile it). Either explain the outage in ¶4 or file the incident under consistency.

Section and paragraph transitions express their declared relationships (e.g. 'An order, then, is made of several things…' additional_support; 'Every arrow in Eva's walk is a message' cause_effect; 'Each of those failures missed a requirement' cause_effect; 'Read the two right-hand columns together' conclusion_summary). The weak joint from the Eva paragraph (p04) into the Noor scene is recorded under flow_is_followable.

results.draft_locus: Promises and Handoffs ¶1
results.quote: Two words describe that pairing and carry the argument of this book: *promise* and *handoff*. This chapter owns their definitions.
results.finding: Both readers mark Promises and Handoffs 'partly unclear': promise was already defined in the steps-table lead-in and handoff in the introduction, so the section reads as a restart; 'This chapter owns their definitions' speaks about the book, not to the reader. Both propose defining the two words before the steps table. The spec's p14 idea and flow rationale (table first, then the words) produce this.
results.corroborated_by: cold_flow_B section 2 (Promises and Handoffs: partly unclear) and item (7)

results.draft_locus: One Order, Three Status Lines ¶3
results.quote: Kestrel & Pine's **Three-Status Order**, #1052877 (named for the three systems that each showed a different status), shows what happens when even one line is flattened
results.finding: Both readers mark One Order, Three Status Lines 'partly unclear': a section about three status lines (money, goods, returns) illustrates them with an incident named for three systems' views of the goods line alone, so readers conflated lines and systems.
results.corroborated_by: cold_flow_B section 2 (One Order, Three Status Lines: partly unclear) and item (8)

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong at Each Step ¶1
results.quote: The same failures can be listed along the journey.
results.finding: Both readers mark When It Goes Wrong at Each Step 'partly unclear': after idempotency and reconciliation were given as the answer, the section returns to listing failures, and its purpose (detection and recovery) appears only at 'Read the two right-hand columns together'. Both propose placing it before the remedy paragraph or before the four-way analysis; the spec's flow rationale fixes the current order.
results.corroborated_by: cold_flow_B section 2 (When It Goes Wrong: partly unclear) and item (12)

results.draft_locus: Introduction callout (failure patterns)
results.quote: The Phantom Stock — the first promise in the journey, 'in stock', is made by the storefront from a warehouse number that can be up to two hours old.
results.finding: The callout says the storefront's stock figure is up to two hours old; the walk says up to an hour and a quarter; two hours belongs to the marketplaces on Black Friday. Both readers stopped to reconcile the figures; as written they disagree about the storefront.

results.draft_locus: Introduction callout (failure patterns)
results.quote: Schrödinger's Order — the order's three status lines live in three systems, and an integration that flattens them into one word makes them disagree.
results.finding: The failure-pattern names in the callout (Schrödinger's Order, The Message in a Bottle) never appear in the body, which tells the incidents under other names (Three-Status Order, Double Refund); readers had to guess which incident instantiates which pattern. Name the pattern at least once where its incident is told.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶4
results.quote: **Where we are in the order's journey.** Eva Janssen buys a jacket and socks from Kestrel & Pine, the fictional outdoor brand used throughout this book.
results.finding: The Eva paragraph, labelled as if the walk were starting, is followed by a scene about Noor in January 2027; Eva does not return for five sections, and the '[[part-9]]' pointer means nothing in chapter 1. Both readers propose moving Eva's introduction to the end of the scene, where 'This chapter does the same with one order…' already introduces her.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Four Drawings of One Order ¶5
results.quote: Six of the seven keep their own record of the order or of their part of it: the **shop platform** from Milan's drawing (its customer-facing pages are the **storefront**), the payment provider (collects the money), the warehouse management system or **WMS** (runs picking and shipping), the ERP, the carrier, PostNL (delivers the parcel and reports its scans), and the returns portal (accepts return requests).
results.finding: Both readers had to count the list to confirm six: nested parenthetical definitions break it up and 'the carrier, PostNL' reads as two items. B also notes the key points list the storefront as a separate system while this sentence makes it part of the shop platform.

results.draft_locus: The Journey in Thirteen Steps ¶1
results.quote: who usually has to keep it: one of the systems above, or a function inside one.
results.finding: The table's 'who must keep it' column names functions (Product information, search; Pricing, inventory, delivery promise) that readers could not match to any of the seven systems just listed; only the walk later shows they live in the shop platform.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶2
results.quote: An online order passes through about a dozen steps
results.finding: The key points say thirteen steps, the next paragraph 'about a dozen'; both readers stopped to check whether these were different lists. The spec's p02 idea and bridge say 'about a dozen' while the thesis says thirteen.

results.draft_locus: Eva's Jacket, System by System ¶6
results.quote: Strictly, the shop platform created order #1072455 a moment before the iDEAL result arrived, with the payment *pending*, and the webhook then marked it paid; steps 5 and 6 overlap.
results.finding: Step 6 corrects the order of events just narrated in step 5, so both readers went back to rebuild the sequence (recovered on second pass). The spec's p28/p29 split puts the pending creation after the payment step.

results.draft_locus: Why the Joins Are Where Things Break ¶6
results.quote: The four ways do not map one to one onto these requirements: a late message can break freshness or speed, a duplicated one consistency.
results.finding: Right after four failure modes, readers meet four requirements and are told the two sets do not correspond; both re-read to see why the requirements were introduced, and freshness vs speed looked like the same thing until the table. The spec's p17 controlling idea requires this sentence.

results.draft_locus: Eva's Jacket, System by System ¶6
results.quote: published an order event to the iPaaS
results.finding: 'Event' (order event, event identifier, inspection event) is never defined, yet the payment evidence and the Established takeaway rest on 'track event identifiers' / 'deduplicate by event identifier'. Guessable as a kind of message for this audience; minor.

The terms Part I relies on are defined at or before first load-bearing use: handoff (Introduction ¶2), promise (steps-table lead-in, with examples in ¶2), status line (Three Status Lines ¶1), system (Scene ¶5); does_not_know terms (ERP, WMS, iPaaS, PSP, webhook, EDI, theme, fulfillment order, SKU/variant, VAT, SaaS, 3PL, IFRS, marketplace connector, idempotency, reconciliation, system of record) are explained in the same sentence where introduced.
Opens on a concrete scenario (pick list, invoice, service ticket), states the thesis and gives a roadmap; no dictionary opening, throat-clearing or announced-topic-only pattern.
The conclusion sorts claims as established / depends on context / author's synthesis and ends with questions and a hand-off; no bare restatement or 'in conclusion' summary.

Synthesis: judge a platform by its handoffs, compare and safely resend contain all four failures. So-what: the table of what each system knows at each moment is 'the cheapest architecture document a merchant can produce' and shows where to look first.

Calls back to the four drawings: 'I follow one real order through every system with a notebook, as Noor did', and Question 1 asks whether someone can draw the path between the systems with each handoff's message and owner.

The intro-only reader predicted, in order: the four drawings; the steps, promise and handoff, the order's entities and three status lines; one order followed through the systems; the four message failures and the checks (reconciliation, idempotency); vendor documentation and law; what changes with growth. This matches every roadmap promise and the expected answer; evidence (one running example, figures, vendor/legal sources) also predicted.

Reader names the WMS-to-shop-platform shipment handoff carried by the iPaaS, the goods line flattened by a partial shipment (Three-Status Order), and that each system is right about its own part; matches expected (goods line between warehouse and storefront, separated from money and returns). Residual uncertainty: how carrier scans reach the shop platform.

Reader names a duplicated message (Double Refund: two senders, no shared record), reconciliation (returns vs refunds) to detect and idempotency to stop a second effect; matches expected. The reader's doubt about the table filing the Double Refund under 'receiver is down' is recorded under evidence_is_explained.
